title: Global Sodium Consumption and Death from Cardiovascular Causes
abstract: BACKGROUND: High sodium intake increases blood pressure, a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, but the effects of sodium intake on global cardiovascular mortality are uncertain. METHODS: We collected data from surveys on sodium intake as determined by urinary excretion and diet in persons from 66 countries (accounting for 74.1% of adults throughout the world), and we used these data to quantify the global consumption of sodium according to age, sex, and country. The effects of sodium on blood pressure, according to age, race, and the presence or absence of hypertension, were calculated from data in a new meta-analysis of 107 randomized interventions, and the effects of blood pressure on cardiovascular mortality, according to age, were calculated from a meta-analysis of cohorts. Cause-specific mortality was derived from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2010. Using comparative risk assessment, we estimated the cardiovascular effects of current sodium intake, as compared with a reference intake of 2.0 g of sodium per day, according to age, sex, and country. RESULTS: In 2010, the estimated mean level of global sodium consumption was 3.95 g per day, and regional mean levels ranged from 2.18 to 5.51 g per day. Globally, 1.65 million annual deaths from cardiovascular causes (95% uncertainty interval [confidence interval], 1.10 million to 2.22 million) were attributed to sodium intake above the reference level; 61.9% of these deaths occurred in men and 38.1% occurred in women. These deaths accounted for nearly 1 of every 10 deaths from cardiovascular causes (9.5%). Four of every 5 deaths (84.3%) occurred in low- and middle-income countries, and 2 of every 5 deaths (40.4%) were premature (before 70 years of age). The rate of death from cardiovascular causes associated with sodium intake above the reference level was highest in the country of Georgia and lowest in Kenya. CONCLUSIONS: In this modeling study, 1.65 million deaths from cardiovascular causes that occurred in 2010 were attributed to sodium consumption above a reference level of 2.0 g per day. (Funded by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.).

claims.text: In 2010, the estimated global mean level of sodium consumption among adults was 3.95 grams per day.
Globally in 2010, 1.65 million annual deaths from cardiovascular causes were attributed to sodium consumption above the reference level of 2.0 grams per day.
Men accounted for 61.9% of cardiovascular deaths attributed to sodium intake above 2.0 grams per day in 2010.
Women accounted for 38.1% of cardiovascular deaths attributed to sodium intake above 2.0 grams per day in 2010.
Cardiovascular deaths attributed to sodium intake above 2.0 grams per day accounted for 9.5% of all global cardiovascular deaths in 2010.
84.3% of cardiovascular deaths attributed to sodium consumption above 2.0 grams per day occurred in low- and middle-income countries.
40.4% of cardiovascular deaths attributed to sodium consumption above 2.0 grams per day occurred prematurely before 70 years of age.
The rate of cardiovascular death associated with sodium intake above 2.0 grams per day was highest in Georgia.
The rate of cardiovascular death associated with sodium intake above 2.0 grams per day was lowest in Kenya.
Each 100 mmol per day reduction in dietary sodium lowers systolic blood pressure by an average of 3.82 mm Hg.
The systolic blood pressure lowering effect of dietary sodium reduction increases significantly with older age.
The systolic blood pressure reduction per unit of sodium restriction is 1.87 mm Hg greater in hypertensive individuals than in normotensive individuals.
The systolic blood pressure reduction per unit of sodium restriction is 2.49 mm Hg greater in Black individuals than in non-Black individuals.

limitations.text: Potential non-blood pressure mediated benefits of sodium reduction, such as reductions in vascular and renal fibrosis, were not incorporated into the disease burden model, which may lead to underestimation of attributable deaths.
Only the effects of blood pressure on cause-specific cardiovascular mortality, rather than non-fatal cardiovascular disease incidence, were considered in the burden calculations.

Prior Cochrane meta-analyses did not evaluate whether blood pressure lowering effects were linear across a wide range of sodium reductions or quantify joint heterogeneity by age, hypertensive status, race, and duration.

future_work.text: Further studies are needed to evaluate clinical cardiovascular disease events and draw definitive conclusions regarding potential additional benefits or harms of more substantial sodium reduction down to 1.5 or 1.0 g per day.

methodologies.name: Global Comparative Risk Assessment Modeling
methodologies.description: Hierarchical Bayesian statistical modeling and comparative risk assessment were used to estimate national, regional, and global sodium consumption and quantify attributable cardiovascular disease mortality using age-, sex-, and country-specific data.
datasets: Dietary recall surveys and food frequency questionnaires
Global Burden of Disease Study 2010 cause-specific mortality database
conditions: Adults aged 20 years and older across 66 countries
Reference sodium intake level of 2.0 ± 0.2 g/day

methodologies.name: Dose-Response Meta-regression of Randomized Controlled Trials
methodologies.description: Inverse-variance weighted multivariate meta-regression of randomized controlled trials was conducted to quantify the effect of sodium reduction on systolic blood pressure across age, race, and hypertensive status.
datasets: 103 randomized controlled trials of sodium reduction with 107 group comparisons
conditions: Mean sodium reduction at least 20 mmol/day
